text:
name: set_reminder
does: Saves a reminder for a time or place and can update it later, like a note to make the salad before guests come or to bring something warm.
inputs: what to remember, and the time or place
people say:
- remind me to make the salad at five
- don't let me forget my umbrella when I leave work
- ping me tomorrow morning about the dentist
- I need a nudge when I get to the shop to buy milk
- move my five o'clock reminder to six

Giannis was not good with technology, so he talked to his tablet instead of touching it. "Please find me a room near the sea for two nights," he said. The tablet showed a long list of hotels. He tried to scroll with one finger, but the list jumped about and he felt lost. "Never mind, just read them to me," he said. The assistant read the first hotel. It was two kilometers from the sea, and the reviews mentioned weak wifi. "That is too far," said Giannis. "Wait, I said two nights, but my brother is coming too. Make it three nights, and a room for two." The assistant changed the search to three nights and two guests, found a hotel right on the beach, and booked it. Giannis smiled. "Good, that is what I meant."

Rafaela was still sleepy when she sat down in the kitchen with her tea. She stirred in some sugar and looked at the old heater on the wall, which made a strange noise. "Please book someone to fix my heater on Monday," she told the speaker. The speaker found a repair shop and booked a visit for Monday morning. A minute later Rafaela said, "Oh, wait. Not Monday. My grandson comes on Monday and the room will be full of people. Make it Tuesday." The speaker moved the visit and said, "Done. The repairman will come on Tuesday at nine." Rafaela nodded, finished her tea, and went to water the plants.

A cup of coffee or tea is something people like to make just right. What changes most is how strong it is and how sweet. People say "make it stronger," "less sugar," or "just a little milk." A smoothie works the same way: you might peel a banana, add some ice, and ask for it thicker or sweeter. On a cold day a sudden wish for something hot can make you order a big tea. Many cafes now let you pick your drink on the internet before you walk in, so it is ready when you arrive. At home you can also ask a voice assistant to start the kettle and make the water extra hot.

Music is for mood. When there is rain outside, many people lie on the sofa and put on soft songs. A playlist is a list of songs that go together, like cool jazz for the evening or loud songs for a run. People change the volume, skip a track they don't like, or ask for another song by the same artist. They say "turn it down," "next one," "play something calmer," or "play that band again." A speaker or a phone listens, does it, and keeps the music going while you do something else.

Neighbours often help each other. If a cat goes missing, someone puts a note on the lamp post or a message in the street group. When you hear about a lost pet or a street party, you can pass it on. People also use these groups to say that a noise is too loud late at night, for example a wireless speaker in the garden. Most people ask politely: "Could you turn it down after ten?" or "Please keep it quiet, the baby is asleep." If you want to help, you can keep your fingers crossed, send a photo of the lost pet, or ask a voice assistant to share the message with the whole street.

name: next_departure
does: Tells you when the next bus or train leaves a stop, such as the one that will drive you past the library, and can plan the round trip home.
inputs: the stop or station, and where you want to go
people say:
- when is the next bus to the library
- what time does my train go
- how long until the number 12 comes
- is the tram late today
- I need to be home by nine, when should I leave

Harriet was making soup in the kitchen, and the blender was loud. She had just split a big onion and her hands were wet. Her thoughts went to the pool outside, because the water had looked green yesterday. "Pool temperature," she said to her phone. The assistant answered, "The pool is twenty-six degrees." Then Harriet said, "Pump status." The assistant checked the pool pump and said it was working and had cleaned the water for two hours this morning. "Good," said Harriet. She asked it to remind her to buy pool chemicals on Saturday, and the assistant put that on her list. Then she went back to her soup.

Person: I just got off work. Can you set the porch lights for six tonight and remind me to buy a tree?
Assistant: Yes. What time should I remind you about the tree?
Person: Four o'clock. And I want a constant light, not the blinking one.
Assistant: Got it, a steady light at six. Should I keep it on all night?
Person: Until ten, then off. Last year's party photos are in the cloud, right?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't see your cloud photos from here. You can open the photo app to check.
Person: Okay, thanks.
Assistant: Rest well. The tree reminder and the steady porch light are both set.

name: check_saved_passwords
does: Goes through your saved logins and unpacks which ones are weak or used twice, then gives the sum of risky ones and tells you if the whole list is safe.
inputs: which password app or saved list to look at
people say:
- are my passwords safe
- which of my logins are too easy to guess
- do I use the same password twice anywhere
- check if any of my passwords leaked
- how weak are my passwords

name: free_up_storage
does: Shows what is filling a phone and lets you pick what to delete, such as a dirty pile of old screenshots, copies of the same photo and long videos of barbecue smoke.
inputs: the kind of file to look at, like photos, videos or apps
people say:
- my phone says storage is full
- I can't take any more pictures
- what is taking up all the space
- get rid of the old screenshots
- why is my phone so slow and full

Thabo sat at his desk with a blank canvas, a brush and a juicy orange. He typed to his phone: "find a video on how to stretch a canvas and set a timer for 20 min". The phone found a short video and started a twenty-minute timer. While the video played, Thabo learned how to pull the cloth tight over the wooden frame. He wanted to paint a portrait of his sister, and the hardest part would be her curly hair. When the timer rang, the assistant said, "Twenty minutes are up." Thabo wiped the orange juice off his fingers and picked up his brush.

It was a cold morning in November, and Mia had just come home from a long night shift. She opened the fridge. There were only a few eggs left and no milk. "Add milk and eggs to my shopping list," she told the kitchen speaker. "But not bread. I don't want bread, we still have some." The speaker added milk and eggs and said, "I did not add bread." Mia also asked for soup ingredients, because she would enjoy a hot bowl after she slept. The speaker added carrots and onions to the list. Mia yawned, thanked it, and went to bed.

Maria was cooking pasta while the kids ran around the kitchen. The speaker was playing songs from an online radio station, and it was very loud. "Make it half as loud," she said. The speaker lowered the volume to half. Then she said, "Set a timer for ten minutes." The speaker set a ten-minute timer. When it rang, the speaker said, "Ten minutes are up," and Maria drained the pasta. "Now stop the music," she said with a smile, "the kids want to hear a story." The speaker stopped the music and the kitchen went quiet.

Alejandro had just moved to a new city. His parents were coming for a vacation and he wanted them to feel safe. In the hall, the smoke alarm began to beep. He said to his phone, "Excuse me, could you please tell me what kind of battery a smoke alarm usually needs and where I can buy one near me, because I am new here, my parents arrive on Friday, and I want the flat to be comfortable and safe for them?" The assistant said most alarms use a nine-volt battery, but he should check the old one to be sure the new one would fit. It then added "9-volt battery" to his shopping list and showed two shops nearby that open early.

A cycling app is a little notebook for your rides. It records the route, the distance, and how fast you went. Some people ride after a morning jog, and the app can sync with a watch so both are saved together. People change what they see: the distance in miles or kilometres, the map with a big zoom, or the speed on each hill. They say things like "how far did I ride today," "show me last week's rides," or "what was my fastest time." Before a ride they might ask for a route that avoids busy roads. After it, they send the map to a friend.

They want to know when the next match begins.
When does the game start?
What time is kickoff tonight?
Is the silver team playing today?
Could you check if the game still goes ahead in the snow?
I hope I don't miss the start of the match tonight.
My dad keeps asking if the game is on yet.
Tell me the time, please.
Would you mind telling me the starting time of the big game on Saturday?

Noah was at the market, looking at a tiny jar of saffron. It was a pricey spice, and he started to worry about money. He took out his phone and typed fast: "how much have i spnt on food this month". The assistant added up his food payments and answered, "You have spent 340 dollars on food so far this month, and your budget is 400." That did not cheer Noah up much. "Ok, so skip the saffron," he said. The assistant took the saffron off his list and told him there were sixty dollars left for the month. Noah bought a cheaper pepper and went home.

Simon woke up in the middle of the afternoon after a late night. His laptop screen was black. "Restart the computer and open the folder with my bicycle photos," he mumbled to the assistant. The computer restarted, and a minute later the folder opened on the screen. There was also a message on the screen: an invite to his cousin's party on Sunday. "Say yes to the invite," he said, and the assistant sent the reply. Then Simon made some coffee and started to look through the photos.

Walter was in the library, wearing one glove because his hand was cold. He had a stale sandwich in his bag and an essay due soon. The text on the page was tiny. He typed to his phone: "make the text biger and read this page out loud". The phone made the letters bigger and began to read the page into his earphones in a calm voice. "Use a slower voice," Walter whispered, and the phone slowed down. He ate a bite of the sandwich, picked up his pen, and took notes while the page was read to him.

A photo is a small memory you can keep. You take one with a phone, and it goes into an album with the others, like a thick book of pictures you carry in your pocket. People take photos of a cat on the sofa, a meal, or a friend's birthday. Then they change things: they crop a picture, make it brighter, or send it to family. They say "share this with Mum," "make a new album called holiday," or "take a screenshot." Some phones listen for a word like "cheese" and take the picture by voice, which helps when your hands are full or the phone is far away.

Person: I need movers for Saturday.
Assistant: Sure. What is the address you are moving to?
Person: 14 Willow Road. Sorry, no, it is 41 Willow Road.
Assistant: Got it, 41 Willow Road. How many rooms need to be packed?
Person: Three bedrooms and a long hallway full of boxes. My sister will fly in to help, so maybe we only need two movers.
Assistant: Okay, two movers on Saturday. Do you want me to send your new address to your children's school?
Person: Yes, please tell the teacher, and write it as 41 Willow Road.
Assistant: Done. I booked two movers for Saturday and sent the new address to the school.

They want to move a meeting to a later time. The direction is always later, and they want a fresh slot.
Push my four o'clock back an hour, but don't cancel it.
Move the team call later today, not to tomorrow.
Can you shift my meeting to the afternoon?
I have to get the groceries home before the ice cream melts, so move my call to five and don't make it any earlier.
Not tomorrow morning, put the dentist after lunch.
Make my meeting later, please, I don't want to rush.
Would you mind finding a different time for Friday's meeting? Not before noon, I wouldn't make it.

Meal planning means deciding what you will eat for the week before you go shopping. It helps you save money and avoid the question of what to cook every night. Some people plan around a low sugar diet, some pack lunches for school, and some want a big dinner after a swim at the pool. A plan might say pasta on Monday, soup on Tuesday, and leftovers on Wednesday. People change it by saying "swap Tuesday and Thursday," "no meat on Friday," or "I want something quick tonight." A good assistant tries to understand what you like and then makes a shopping list for the meals.

They want to know when an assignment is due.
When is my science homework due?
What's due on the twelfth of March?
Do I have anything online to hand in this week?
Cast an eye over my list and tell me which essay comes first.
When do I have to finish the engine project?
Tell me the deadline for the history report, please.
I think I forgot something, what is due before the twelfth of March?
Could you please check which homework is due on the twelfth of March and tell me if any of it must be handed in on paper?

Marlene was stopped at a red light when her phone buzzed. She sneezed and then said, "Read my new messages out loud and make the text bigger on the screen." The phone read the first message: it was a booking confirmation from the garage for her car on Thursday. The text on the screen grew bigger, but the voice was very quiet, set at the minimum volume. "Turn it up," she said. The assistant raised the volume and read the next message, and the light turned green.

name: check_door_lock
does: Tells you if the front, back or garage door is locked and locks it for you, which helps when you stay at a hotel or leave the house on a sunny morning in a hurry.
inputs: which door to check
people say:
- did I lock the front door
- make sure the garage is shut
- I left in a rush, is the house locked
- is the back door open
- lock up for me, I'm already on the bus

Dana had just moved to the city and wanted to cook something simple. She had half a loaf of stale bread. "How long do I bake bread pudding at 200 degrees?" she asked the kitchen speaker. Then she changed her mind. "Wait, I meant 180 degrees." The speaker said, "At 180 degrees, bread pudding takes about forty minutes," and it started a timer. Dana switched on the oven light and watched the pudding. The doorbell rang, so she said, "Pause the timer." Five minutes later she came back and said, "Resume the timer." The speaker started it again.

Mehmet worked in a restaurant kitchen and came home tired. The shower water was only lukewarm, and the family-size water heater, which sits in the cellar, seemed to be failing. "Could you please check if the water heater is working, because the shower has been cold since this morning and my wife wants a bath when she gets home?" he asked. The assistant said the heater was on but set too low, at forty degrees. It raised it to fifty-five. Then it said a sensor had found a small leak near the west wall and offered to book a plumber. Mehmet said yes.

A focus timer helps you work without drifting. You pick a time, like twenty-five minutes, and work until it rings. Then you take a short break and pull yourself away from the screen. People use timers to remember an appointment, to cook, or to study. Some timers turn red when the time is nearly up. Routines work the same way: a morning routine might list wake up, wash, breakfast, and leave. People change them by saying "make my break five minutes longer," "start a thirty-minute timer," or "remind me to stand up every hour."

Emre woke up cold in a hotel room he did not know. The window was open, and the floor was chilly. He rubbed his eyes and said to the room tablet, "Check-in time?" The tablet said, "Check-in starts at three, and check-out is at eleven." He did not understand the second part, so he asked, "What does that mean?" The tablet explained that he had to leave the room by eleven. Emre then said, "Late checkout?" and the tablet asked the front desk, which gave him until noon. He smiled and closed the window.

Babies like a plan. They eat, sleep and play at about the same times each day, so parents keep a simple schedule. A feeding might be every three hours, and a nap after lunch. Some parents keep a file of notes on how much the baby ate and slept. A baby monitor lets you hear and see the room when you are in another one. People change the times by saying "move the nap to two," "remind me about the bottle at six," or "turn on the monitor." It is easy to forget things when you are tired, so many parents ask an assistant to remember them. Many babies also have a favorite song to fall asleep to.

They want the heat turned up.
Turn up the heating and close the blinds.
It's chilly in here, can you warm up the living room and turn on the radiator in the hall?
Put the thermostat at twenty-two and keep it there.
I'm bored of sitting in this cold room, make it warmer.
The boiler repair is finished, so please turn the heating on and set it to twenty degrees.
We go to the cinema at eight, so heat the house now and turn it down later.
Bump it up two degrees, please.
Would you mind making the bedroom warmer and telling me what the temperature is now?

Person: Change password.
Assistant: Sure. Which account, your email or your phone?
Person: Email. I'm hungry, so be quick.
Assistant: No problem. Do you want me to make a new one for you, or will you type it?
Person: Make one. Tell me what it is.
Assistant: I can't read a password out loud for safety, but I can save it in your password app. A sentence of four random words is easy to remember and hard to guess.
Person: Okay, save it.
Assistant: Done. Your new email password is saved.

Person: Share the park photos with my mum and write a little note under them.
Assistant: Happy to. Which album are the park photos in?
Person: The one called Sunday. The kids are on the slide, so it's very busy in the pictures.
Assistant: Found it. What should the note say?
Person: Write: Such a calm afternoon after all.
Assistant: Done. I shared the album with your mum with that note. Do you also want a copy on the big screen in the living room?
Person: Can you print them too?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't print photos. I can send them to a print shop's app if you tell me which one.

They want a reminder to take a short break.
Remind me to take a break in ten minutes. No wait, fifteen.
Tell me when to stop and stretch.
I don't care when, just make sure I get up for a few minutes.
Break timer, twenty minutes. Actually, make it thirty.
I've been at my desk for hours, nudge me to rest soon.
I don't want to be rude, but please stop me before this week's meeting runs over.
Set a pause for five o'clock, no, half past four.
Could you please remind me every hour this week to stand up and walk around?

A dishwasher is a machine that cleans plates and cups for you. You load it, add soap, pick a program, and let it run. Some programs are quick, and some use more heat for dirty pans. People change the program, the start time, or the strength. They say "start the dishwasher after dinner," "use the short wash," or "stop it for a moment." On a stormy night, some people wait to run it, because a power cut would stop the cycle. The same goes for a washing machine when you have a big pile of laundry. A voice assistant can start either one, if they are connected.

Giulia owned a small flower shop. Tonight her sister would lock up, so Giulia wanted the alarm set. "Turn on the shop camera and the door alarm, but don't record inside the back room," she told the assistant. The assistant turned on the front camera and the door alarm and left the back room camera off. "Is that correct?" it asked. "Yes, that is correct," said Giulia. She added, "And I don't want alerts for the cat at night. I only want to hear about people." The assistant set the camera to send an alert only when it could notice a person. Giulia smiled, waved goodbye, and went home.

Ursula was baking bread and a yogurt cake at the same time, and her kids came into the kitchen to join her. "Set the oven for 180 degrees and give me an hourly reminder about the dough," she said. The oven began to heat up, and the assistant said, "The oven is on. I will remind you every hour." After an hour the speaker said, "Time to check the dough." It had risen well, and the kids pressed it gently with their fingers. Ursula laughed and put the cake in the oven.

A kettle is a good example of a simple kitchen machine. You fill it with water, put it on its base, plug it in, and press a button. It boils the water and clicks off by itself. People use it for tea, soup, or instant noodles. Some kettles let you pick the heat, from warm to boiling. People change that by saying "heat the water to eighty degrees" or "make it boil." If the kettle is new, you may need to dig out the manual to see how. A smart kettle can start when you say "put the kettle on," so the water is ready when you walk in.

Person: Switch off the outlet next to my desk next Tuesday at noon.
Assistant: Which outlet do you mean? I see two in your room.
Person: The one with the purple plug in it.
Assistant: Got it. Should it stay off, or come back on later?
Person: Back on at six.
Assistant: Done. The outlet by your desk will turn off next Tuesday at noon and on again at six.
Person: Can you tap into my neighbour's solar panels to save power?
Assistant: Sorry, I can't do that. I can only help with your own devices. I can show how much power your room uses, if you like.

name: track_food_order
does: Shows where your food order is and how long it will take before your hobby club meeting, and can send the driver an urgent note, like the gate code, or tweet a thank you to the restaurant.
inputs: the restaurant or order, and the note for the driver if there is one
people say:
- where is my pizza
- how long until the food gets here
- tell the driver to leave it at the back door
- my dinner is late, can you check it
- will the food arrive before eight, my club starts then

Keoni had just moved to the city and knew almost nobody. He was carrying a water bottle in one hand and a bag in the other. "Call my landlord and tell me how many minutes I have left on my monthly plan," he told his phone. The phone called the landlord and put him on speakerphone, so Keoni could talk while he walked. After the call the assistant said, "Your monthly plan has 100 minutes left. Based on how you talk, I estimate you will use them all in about ten days." Keoni thanked it and decided to send more messages instead.

Daniel was not good with technology, and his new smart lock confused him. He stood by the iron gate with an electric bill in his hand and felt sad, because he did not know how to lock up. "Hello? Can you lock the front door but not the garage? I don't want the garage locked, my son still has to come in," he said slowly to the little speaker. The speaker answered, "I locked the front door. The garage is still open." Daniel breathed out and smiled. It had been easier than he thought.

They want to know their current medicine dose.
My dose?
How much do I take?
What is my dose now?
How many pills today?
Tell me how much of the cherry cough syrup I should take.
I spend too long reading the label, can you say what my dose is?
What am I supposed to take at night?
Could you please remind me how many spoons of my medicine I should take each morning?

Lucia spent most of her day in the car. Today she wanted to hear about the train delays on the radio. "Tune in to the news station tomorrow morning at seven," she told the car assistant. The assistant saved the station and said the radio would turn on at seven. Then Lucia added, "Tonight after dinner, play the monthly music show on my favorite station." The assistant set a second reminder for the show. Lucia smiled, because now she would not have to search for either one while driving.

Mathieu was texting on the sofa when he looked in the fridge and found only a lemon. He typed to his phone assistant, "we're out of milk and cereal again lol". The assistant understood and added milk and cereal to the shopping list. "Want me to remind you when you're near the shop?" it asked. "Yes," Mathieu typed. He had a receipt from last week in his pocket and took a photo of it so he would remember the prices. Later he would visit the supermarket on the east side of town, and the phone buzzed with the list when he arrived.

name: bedtime_routine
does: Walks a child through the evening steps, like bathe, brush teeth, a short story and quiet radio music, and tells the parent when each step starts.
inputs: the child's bedtime and which steps to include
people say:
- start the kids' bedtime routine
- it's almost eight, get them ready for bed
- time for bath and teeth, then a story
- tell Max it's bedtime in ten minutes
- I want the little ones in bed by half past seven

Tamar was texting her friends about dinner. "Can you book a table for four at the noodle place this Saturday afternoon? We just want to chill, nothing fancy," she asked her phone. The phone checked the restaurant and found a table at three o'clock. It booked it and sent the details to her friends. Tamar also asked, "Is the service fast? We only have an hour." The assistant said the reviews call the service fast, and it added that the menu sells water by the liter, which made Tamar laugh.

Clocks tell us what time it is, and time zones tell us that the time is different in other places. When it is noon in London, it is often seven in the morning in New York. Long ago people used a pencil to write down the time on a paper chart; now a phone keeps it. Most phones pick the right time for where you are, but you can add other cities. People ask "what time is it in Tokyo," "is it morning in Sydney," or "set my clock to home time." Even on a trip, your home city can stay as a permanent clock on the screen.
